title: A hymn in Jaitsri
hook: Guru Arjan's Var in Jaitsri opens with a salok: whole at the beginning, the middle and the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Jaitsri, the jewel in the heart and the Guru's hand on the forehead, and your line was quiet strength. Whom did you steady without fixing anything? Day one thousand eighty-seven.

Beginning, middle, end. Somewhere in school, someone drew those three words on a board and said every story has them. The beginning is full of promise. The middle sags; it's where people get lost, bored, or stuck. The end, if it's a good one, ties things up. A lot of life happens in some middle or other. Near the end of the Jaitsri section, Guru Arjan begins a Var, a ballad, and its very first salok takes those three words and says something surprising about each one. Today: a hymn in Jaitsri, and a middle that isn't missing anything.
screen: `BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.` → `THE MIDDLE SAGS.` → `A VAR BEGINS IN JAITSRI.`

segments.voice: First, the form. A Var in the Granth is a ballad made of pauris, stanzas, with saloks, short verses, set before them. The saloks are like small lamps carried ahead of each stanza. This one, Jaitsri ki Var, is Guru Arjan's, mahala five. Now the opening salok. It begins: aad pooran, madh pooran, ant pooran, parmesurah. Aad: the beginning. Madh: the middle. Ant: the end. Pooran: full, whole, complete. In paraphrase: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end, is the Supreme Lord. Then it goes on: the saints remember the one who pervades everywhere, and Nanak calls that one the destroyer of wrongs, the Lord of the world. Look at the word in the middle. Madh pooran. Whole in the middle. That's the part of any story where we feel least whole: the middle of a long illness, the middle of a degree, the middle of grief, the middle of an ordinary Wednesday. The salok doesn't say God is waiting at the end once you get through it. It says the middle is just as full as the start and the finish. That's where the strength in this Var comes from. Not a burst of courage for the big moment, but a fullness that doesn't thin out halfway. The Var goes on, stanza by stanza, and it's built on that first promise. Strength in jaitsri is the strength of the middle. Today's line.
screen: `A VAR: STANZAS WITH SALOKS BEFORE THEM.` · `AAD, MADH, ANT: BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.` · `POORAN: WHOLE, AT EVERY POINT.` · `THE MIDDLE IS FULL TOO.` · then, large: `STRENGTH IN JAITSRI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in the middle. If you can, play a recording of Jaitsri ki Var, or any Jaitsri shabad, first. Then sit. Notice the beginning of a breath, the cool air coming in. Notice the end of it, the warm air going out. Now notice the middle: the small pause at the top, where nothing seems to be happening. Rest there, breath after breath. Then think of one thing in your life that's in its middle right now, unfinished, and let it be whole for the length of a breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in each pause. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Jaitsri. Guru Arjan's Var, which opens with a salok: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end. Today's word.
Your line: strength in jaitsri. Pick one task you're in the middle of today, and give it one unhurried minute, as if the middle were the point. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Jaitsri ki Var is sung in kirtan with its saloks and pauris, and its opening salok, aad pooran madh pooran ant pooran, is sung and recited in gurdwaras and at home.
